cue: Hold the phone close to the ground and turn it slowly. A woodlouse heads for the darker side.

cpd.note: measured in one fiddler crab and drawn for every decapod

rate.note: 60 over 73.6 is 0.82; a crayfish's movement fibres follow only about 10 Hz and were not used

field.note: inferred from facet counts; no resolution is measured in a woodlouse

crab_protan.note: Vienot, Brettel and Mollon 1999, as in the squirrel view; entered from memory

overlay.name: shadow
overlay.note: when the light falls suddenly, a dark ring runs out from where it fell (atlas 14); woodlice turn toward dark shelter

rows: Two small-eyed water isopods have 4 and about 25 facets to an eye, and a close picture of a Rough Woodlouse’s eye shows 22. The Asian shore crab has 2,400 to 6,000.
The sea slater, a big-eyed seashore relative, has facets about 7 degrees apart, which resolves about 0.07 cycles per degree, near an eight-hundredth of your 60.
With about twenty facets to an eye, a woodlouse is drawn with no image at all, only how much light there is and from where.
Woodlice turn away from light toward dark shelters, where the air is damper and cooler.
Woodlice shelter more when the air is dry, and huddled together they lose about half as much water as they do alone.
About six in ten Common Pill Woodlice are active at night, against nine in ten of Philoscia muscorum, the fourth most recorded woodlouse.
No measurement of a woodlouse’s colour sense was found, so the picture is grey.
How far and how evenly a woodlouse walks changes with the dampness of the air, which a camera cannot show.
With &draw=shadow, a sudden fall of light sends a dark ring across the picture. The ring is the app's drawing.

rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: If you are a European woodlouse (Porcellio scaber), your eyes are made of many small units, and each unit has its own curved lens with a round crystalline cone beneath it. Other Porcellio woodlice very likely have the same kind of eye. For most other woodlice and relatives, nobody has examined the eye, so its kind is unknown.
rows.note: R2 also names Armadillidium vulgare, but the view marks its eye type unknown, so I stated it only for Porcellio scaber. R1 is a skink and was not used.

rows.title: Dark
rows.text: Nobody has measured how your eyes guide you toward dark places. Nobody has measured how much light it takes to change what you do, in any woodlouse or its close relatives.
rows.note: Only record (R1) is a rattlesnake study and says nothing about woodlice, so I wrote an i row with no claims and no citations.

rows.title: Night
rows.text: On a dark night in the field, about 60% of common pill-bugs were out and active. If you are another pill-bug of the genus Armadillidium, you very likely are active at night as well, since the common pill-bug is your relative. For most other woodlice, nobody has measured it.
rows.note: Dropped the 40% figure. R2's value also lists 92% for Philoscia muscorum, but its quote states only the 60% figure, so I left that out.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of a woodlouse. In the wharf roach, an isopod related to you that lives on shores, a compilation of measurements lists three kinds, and one of them senses ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see. Nobody knows whether you have the same three.
rows.note: Left out the 340, 470 and 520 nm values because they belong to the wharf roach alone. R1 and R4 are lizard records and were not used.
